title: Conditional Probability
body:
$$
P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}, \qquad P(B) > 0
$$

"The probability of $A$ **given that** $B$ happened." The mechanics are simple and the picture is
simpler: **learning $B$ occurred throws away everything outside $B$ and renormalises what is left.**
$B$ becomes the new sample space, which is why you divide by $P(B)$, and it is why conditional
probabilities are ordinary probabilities on a smaller universe. All three axioms in [[Probability]]
still hold for $P(\cdot \mid B)$.

## The multiplication rule

Rearranged, the definition is the rule you actually use:

$$
P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)\,P(B) = P(B \mid A)\,P(A)
$$

and it chains to any length, $P(A \cap B \cap C) = P(A)P(B \mid A)P(C \mid A \cap B)$. This is what
makes sequential problems (drawing cards without replacement, a fault propagating through stages)
tractable: work along the tree, multiply as you go.

## Independence

$A$ and $B$ are **independent** when knowing one tells you nothing about the other:

$$
P(A \mid B) = P(A)
\iff
P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)
$$

The second form is the definition worth keeping, because it is symmetric and it survives $P(B) = 0$.

**Independence is a property to be checked, not assumed**, and it is the assumption almost every
formula in the rest of the course quietly needs: $\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y)$
in [[Variance]], the $n$ trials of a [[Probability Distribution|binomial]], the sample in the
[[Central Limit Theorem]], the cells of a [[Chi-Square Test]]. When it fails, the arithmetic does
not warn you; it just gives the wrong answer with confident-looking error bars.

> [!warning] Mutually exclusive is not independent
> They are close to opposite. If $A$ and $B$ are disjoint and both have non-zero probability then
> $P(A \mid B) = 0 \neq P(A)$, so they are maximally **dependent**: $B$ occurring rules $A$ out
> entirely. Disjoint is a statement about the sets, independent is a statement about the
> probabilities, and no dataset makes both true unless one event is impossible.

## Law of total probability

If $B_1, \dots, B_k$ partition the sample space:

$$
P(A) = \sum_{i} P(A \mid B_i)\,P(B_i)
$$

Split the world into cases, work out $A$ within each, and weight by how likely each case was. This
is the denominator of [[Bayes Theorem]] and it is how almost every non-trivial probability in the
course is computed.

```
Two machines make widgets. Machine 1 makes 70% with a 2% defect rate,
machine 2 makes 30% with a 5% defect rate.

P(defective) = (0.02)(0.70) + (0.05)(0.30) = 0.014 + 0.015 = 0.029
```

Note that the smaller machine contributes more defects than the larger one. Reversing that
calculation, asking which machine a given defective widget came from, is exactly what
[[Bayes Theorem]] does.

## Conditional independence

$A$ and $B$ can be dependent overall and independent once you condition on $C$, or the reverse.
Both directions happen, and confusing them produces Simpson's paradox, where a trend present in
every subgroup reverses when the groups are pooled. It is also the assumption naive Bayes
classifiers in [[MACHINE LEARNING]] are named for: features are taken to be independent *given the
class*, which is usually false and works anyway.
